candidates.title: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (CCS: Security and privacy / Computing methodologies - AI); not yet indexed by Semantic Scholar
candidates.citationVelocity: submitted 11 Nov 2026 (3 days), too new for citation data
candidates.institution: Vulcan Research / AIFT Singapore; Keio University Global Research Institute; Standard Chartered India
communitySignals: Papers with Code: no repo found via search; code released on GitHub by authors (VulcanLab/guardscope)
credibilityEvidence: Section 3 enumerates 15 action paths and 8 topology designs derived bottom-up from real deployed systems (Table 1-4)

Section 4-5 two-stage framework (static source analysis + empirical kernel-ground-truth measurement via Tracee eBPF) evaluated against real production controls (Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit, agentgateway) across two independent harnesses (Pi, OpenClaw)
Section 6 states limitations explicitly (referenced); related work section systematically positions against 5 categories of prior enforcement/monitoring work
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers design derivation, static+empirical measurement methodology, and real-control evaluation with reproducibility controls (digest pinning, readiness gates); not yet externally replicated since it is 3 days old
reproducibilityEvidence: Code and Docker Compose fixtures released at github.com/VulcanLab/guardscope
Run manifests pin harness/control/workload/sensor images by digest for reproducible re-runs
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Narrow, falsifiable claim (coverage measurement framework + finding that gateway-only controls miss most of the 15 action paths) is directly supported by the static+empirical methodology shown
candidates.primaryLimitation: Reference workload only exercises 4 of the 15 enumerated action paths empirically; the remaining paths' coverage outcomes rest on the derived analysis, not kernel-verified runs
candidates.presentationReason: Method, workload, and classification scheme (checked/bypassed/prevented) are precisely defined with explicit evidence trails
candidates.reason: Directly measurable, falsifiable finding with real production security tooling (Microsoft AGT, agentgateway) and kernel ground truth; exposes a concrete enterprise risk (gateway-only controls miss most non-tool-call action paths) that complements the other two selected papers' theme of observable-vs-actual agent behavior

candidates.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint; submitted to Empirical Software Engineering journal (under review); not yet indexed by Semantic Scholar
candidates.citationVelocity: submitted 10 Nov 2026 (4 days), too new for citation data
candidates.institution: Seoul School of Integrated Sciences and Technologies (aSSIST); AIM Intelligence, Seoul
communitySignals: Papers with Code: no repo found via search; replication package released via journal supplementary material
credibilityEvidence: 2,160 episodes across tau2-bench airline/retail domains, every database write recorded (Section 4)
120 episodes independently labeled by two human annotators on three axes (task/policy/commitment correctness), used as ground truth for RQ2 (Section 4.6)
Statistical comparison across 4 evaluators with multiple-comparison correction for the gate experiment (Section 6)
Related work explicitly positions against AgentRewardBench and two independent studies reporting the same phenomenon on tau2-bench
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Large episode count, independent human labeling, and a traced root-cause mechanism (gates' evidence digest drops order-status/auth fields) go beyond a single anecdote; single benchmark family (tau2-bench) and single annotator pair limit generalization
reproducibilityEvidence: Traces, code, prompts, human labels, and adjudication records released per Declarations section
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Claim is narrow and quantified (judge agrees with native scoring 56.2% of the time; passes 10/11 confirmed forbidden writes) and directly backed by the described experiment
candidates.primaryLimitation: Human reference standard covers only 120 of 2,160 episodes, and the benchmark domain (tau2-bench airline/retail) is narrower than general agentic deployments
candidates.presentationReason: Four evaluators, three research questions, and the boundary-evaluator definition are stated precisely with a worked example carried through the paper
candidates.reason: Concrete, numbers-backed warning for anyone using LLM-judge evaluation in production: judges passed 10 of 11 confirmed policy-violating actions even with the policy document attached, while a zero-model-call rule check caught all 11 — directly actionable for teams building or trusting agent eval pipelines, and forms the 'evaluation methodology' angle alongside guardscope's security angle and Breaking Bad's interpretability angle

candidates.title: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CL / cs.AI); not yet indexed by Semantic Scholar
candidates.citationVelocity: submitted 11 Nov 2026 (3 days), too new for citation data
candidates.institution: AI Security Institute (UK AISI); Resolution; ERA:Cambridge
communitySignals: HF Daily Papers: not found (searched; only unrelated reward-hacking papers from earlier in 2026 surfaced)
Papers with Code: no repo found via search
credibilityEvidence: Vector constructed from 1,774 narratives with no hacking examples (Section 3), validated by held-out classification and layer-sweep accuracy
Correlational evidence across 3 models and 3 benchmarks (ImpossibleBench, TACO honeypot, CheatBench) with explicit statistics (AUROC 0.77, Cohen's d, Welch t-test p-values)
Causal steering experiments with dose-response curves and capability-preservation controls (GSM8K/MMLU-Pro checks) distinguishing genuine effect from model degradation (Section 5)
Compares task-badness vector against desperation, task-impossibility, and random-vector controls to isolate the effect
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Combines correlational (activation rises before hack) and causal (steering changes hack rate) evidence across 3 models with appropriate controls; GPT-OSS and Gemma show weaker/partial replication of the pattern, which the paper reports transparently rather than hiding
reproducibilityEvidence: Methodology (vector construction, steering procedure, benchmarks used) is fully specified; no code/data release link found in the fetched abstract/intro sections
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The core claim (a pre-hack internal pressure state exists and is causally linked to hacking in at least 2 of 3 models) is well-supported; cross-model generalization claims are appropriately hedged in the paper itself
candidates.primaryLimitation: Relationship between the vector and hacking differs across models (GPT-OSS separates hacking from honest solves but not from honest failures; Gemma shows the effect on only one of two benchmarks tested), so the mechanism is not yet shown to be universal
candidates.presentationReason: Each experiment states its setup, benchmark, and statistic precisely, and cross-model discrepancies are discussed openly rather than glossed over
candidates.reason: First evidence that a pre-hack internal pressure state exists independent of surface chain-of-thought and can be read and steered directly, giving a monitoring signal that does not depend on models verbalizing their intent to cheat — directly relevant to agent oversight as reasoning traces become less reliable, and completes the 'observable signal vs actual internal/external state' theme with guardscope and the tau2-bench paper
